                    ### Question
                    A 72-year-old man comes to the emergency department because of blurry vision for the past 3 days. He has also had 4 episodes of right-sided headaches over the past month. He has no significant past medical history. His father died of coronary artery disease at the age of 62 years. His temperature is 37.2°C (99°F), pulse is 94/min, and blood pressure is 232/128 mm Hg. Fundoscopy shows right-sided optic disc blurring and retinal hemorrhages. A medication is given immediately. Five minutes later, his pulse is 75/min and blood pressure is 190/105 mm Hg. Which of the following drugs was most likely administered?

                    ### Options

opb. Hydralazine
opc. Fenoldopam
opd. Nicardipine
ope. Nitroprusside

### Enhanced Information (For Contextual Support):
The 72-year-old man presents with blurry vision, headaches, and severely elevated blood pressure (232/128 mm Hg), indicating a possible hypertensive emergency with risk of end-organ damage, as evidenced by optic disc blurring and retinal hemorrhages. Immediate treatment is required to lower blood pressure rapidly. Labetalol and Nitroprusside are both effective for acute blood pressure control. Labetalol is commonly used in hypertensive emergencies due to its rapid action and ability to lower both blood pressure and heart rate, as seen with the pulse decrease to 75/min and blood pressure reduction to 190/105 mm Hg. Nitroprusside is also effective but is typically reserved for more severe cases or when immediate control is critical. Hydralazine, while effective, is slower acting and less preferred for immediate management. Nicardipine and Fenoldopam are less commonly used in acute settings. Given the rapid response in this case, Labetalol is the most likely medication administered.
